title: The crust of flavour
text: Much of what we call cooking is really one chemical reaction, first {{1}} in 1912 by the French doctor Louis-Camille Maillard. When proteins and sugars are heated together above roughly 140 degrees, they begin to {{2}} into hundreds of new compounds that exist in neither raw ingredient. These are the molecules of browned food: the golden {{3}} of a loaf's crust, the dark edge of a roast, the smell of coffee beans cracking in the roaster, the sear on a steak. Heat, in short, {{4}} a small factory of flavour. Cooks guard the conditions carefully. The surface must be dry, because moisture {{5}} the temperature down near boiling point, where browning stalls — which is why recipes {{6}} on patting meat dry before it meets the pan. Cooked too hot, though, the same chemistry turns against the cook: above about 200 degrees the surface begins to {{7}} bitter, acrid compounds instead. The Maillard reaction, in the end, is what {{8}} cooking from merely warming food up.

gaps.explanation: 'first identified in 1912' — discovered and described; a natural reaction can be identified but not invented.
'they begin to combine into hundreds of new compounds' — join chemically; compile is for collections of material, coin is for words.
'the golden hue of the crust' — its colour; the other nouns share the 'hu' spelling but nothing else.
'heat builds a small factory of flavour' — constructs it; burn and buy contradict the sense of creation in the passage.
'moisture holds the temperature down near boiling point' — keeps it there; haul and hurl mean pull and throw.
'recipes insist on patting meat dry' — demand it; persist takes 'in', and assist and resist do not introduce a requirement.
'begins to produce bitter compounds' — generate them; provoke = cause a reaction in someone, profess = claim.
'what separates cooking from warming food up' — distinguishes one from the other; secure takes 'against/for', settle and shelter take different patterns.
